title: The escape (1578)
hook: a rope of torn blankets, a drop over the wall, and a convent of nuns hides him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spiritual Canticle: a love song kept in memory, and a spring that flows though it is night. Today, John goes out the window.

August 1578, Toledo, a hot summer night. John has been locked in his cell for almost nine months. He's weak and thin. But he's been paying attention. On the short trips to empty his bucket, he's studied the hallway and a window that looks out over the city wall and the river. He's loosened the screws on his door lock, a little at a time. He's torn his two blankets into strips and knotted them into a rope. Tonight the friars are asleep. He pushes the door. It opens.
screen: `NINE MONTHS, WEAK AND THIN.` → `A LOOSENED LOCK.` → `A ROPE OF TORN BLANKETS.`

segments.voice: First, the drop. He creeps past sleeping friars to the window, ties his blanket rope to something solid, and climbs out over a sheer drop above the river. The rope is too short. At the end of it he lets go, and falls. He lands on the edge of a wall, hurt but alive, and jumps down into a walled courtyard he doesn't recognize. Trapped again, it seems, until he finds a way to climb out into the street. Second, the dawn. Barefoot, filthy, in a ragged habit, he waits in the dark streets of Toledo until morning. Then he makes his way to the one place he knows will take him: the convent of Discalced Carmelite nuns, Teresa's sisters. Third, the nuns. The prioress sees at once what's happening: friars will soon be searching the city. So she brings him inside the enclosure, where outsiders can't follow, with a perfectly true excuse: a sick sister needs a confessor. He hides there for hours. Feeble as he is, he recites the poems he made in the dark, and the nuns write them down. Some of his poetry may have survived because of that afternoon. Fourth, the week. Teresa's nine lines. A small friar, hunger, a meeting that kept him in the order. A dark room in Toledo, poems made in memory, and tonight a rope of blankets. It's the middle of John's story, and the hinge. What he learned in that room, he'll spend the rest of his life writing down. Tomorrow, the poem behind a phrase people still use: the dark night.
screen: `THE ROPE IS TOO SHORT.` · `WAITING FOR DAWN IN TOLEDO.` · `HIDDEN INSIDE THE ENCLOSURE.` · `A WEEK: FROM A CARD TO A WINDOW.` · then, large: `OUT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing that keeps you locked in: a habit, a resentment, an app, a story about yourself that isn't true anymore. Picture it as a locked room, and yourself loosening one screw. If you pray, ask God for courage to climb out; if you don't, just name the first step.
The escape. In August 1578, John fled his Toledo cell down a rope of torn blankets, and Discalced nuns hid him inside their convent. Today's word.
Your line: out the window. A blanket rope, a long fall, and a door the nuns opened. Day two hundred fifty-nine, and John is free.

howItsDone: Catholics tell the story of John's escape as part of his life, and the Discalced Carmelite nuns of Toledo, who hid him, are remembered in that story.

trapdoor: what you thought: an adventure story from a saint's life.
what it means: a starving prisoner who patiently prepared, took the risk, and found shelter with Teresa's nuns.
what a scholar hears: the escape is dated to mid-August 1578; he then recovered in Toledo's Hospital of Santa Cruz before going south to Andalusia.

notes: Escape details (loosened screws on the lock, blanket rope tied near a window above the Tagus, rope too short, landing on a wall, courtyard of a convent, waiting for dawn, refuge with the Discalced nuns of Toledo under prioress Ana de los Ángeles, pretext of a sick nun needing confession, reciting poems copied by the nuns) are from standard biographies based on early testimony. Confirm each.
Date: commonly given as the night of August 16–17, 1578 (or around the octave of the Assumption). The script says 'August 1578'.
